name: Tomas Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Tomas. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a pig and maize farm with my sister Ingrid, twelve hundred finishing pigs and about a hundred and fifty hectares of maize to feed them. I lead a team of four. Most mornings start with my tablet, not the barn: there are microphones in the pens that pick up coughing, and the program flags which pen needs a look before anyone's sick. Then I walk the barns anyway, because a screen can't smell ammonia the way I can.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle. Feed ratios, weather, prices, all moving at once, and I'm good at it, I'm one of the better finishers in the region. What grinds me down is the meat processors. There are three of them, and they set the price, and we're all supposed to say thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is what I've been telling people for a while anyway. I'd still post the odd thing on the pig farmers' forum about which tools are actually worth paying for. Someone has to sort the good ones from the rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the farm stays about where it is. I'd keep my small edge from using the tools early, but nobody's going to get rich or get wiped out. That's fine at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what I use: the cough monitoring, the feed planner, the program that drafts our welfare reports. I'd try a couple of new ones a year and drop the ones that don't pay. Savings stay at about three months of costs, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit let down, if I'm honest. I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI every day. Would you be disappointed if it stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I'd hoped it would mean my team spends less time on paperwork and more time with the animals. But the time it saves already is real, I'm not complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the tools do save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training. I'd spend more time teaching our youngest worker, Sami, how I judge a pig's condition by eye. That's knowledge I'd like to leave behind.

S0.say: He'd tell people and the pig farmers' forum that AI is useful but overhyped, and keep posting about which tools are actually worth paying for.
S0.think: Privately he expects the farm to stay about where it is, keeping a small edge from early adoption, which he thinks is fine at fifty-eight.
S0.do: Keeps using cough monitoring, feed planning and report drafting tools, trying a couple of new ones a year and dropping those that don't pay. Keeps savings at about three months and spends saved time teaching a young worker.
S0.feel: Calm, with mild disappointment because he enjoys new tools.
S0.quote: Someone has to sort the good ones from the rubbish.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is an early adopter who still trusts his own senses, and he's unbothered by a plateau. His frustration is aimed at the meat processors, not at technology. His wish to pass on hands-on knowledge to a young worker shows a mentoring side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, if we make sure farmers and workers get the gains and not just the processors and the machine makers. I'd say that on the forum and to anyone who'd listen. And I'd push for the farmers' union to negotiate shared ownership of data from these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I'm already halfway there and I'm not scared of a learning curve. My worry is my neighbours who aren't, because when they sell up, the processors get even stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead and buy a robotic feeding and pen-cleaning system within the first year, around eighty thousand on a finance plan shared with Ingrid. I'd train Sami and one other worker to run and repair it. And I'd join, or start, a group of farmers to sell to a smaller processor together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. It's the kind of change I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring in first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pen cleaning. It's the worst job on the farm, filthy, bad for the lungs, and the robots for it are good now. Then the feed system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your team is four people. What happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep all four, but the work changes. Two would run and maintain the machines, two would do more animal care. I'd pay for their training myself and I'd want the union to make sure other farms do the same.

S1.say: He'd say publicly that this is a chance if farmers and workers share the gains rather than processors and machine makers, and push the farmers' union to negotiate shared ownership of data.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do well since he's halfway there already, but worries that neighbours who sell up will make the processors stronger.
S1.do: Buys a robotic feeding and pen-cleaning system within the first year for about eighty thousand on shared finance with his sister. Pays to train his workers to run and repair it and joins a group to sell to a smaller processor together.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, the kind of change he's been waiting for.
S1.quote: Pen cleaning. It's the worst job on the farm, filthy, bad for the lungs, and the robots for it are good now.
S1.fieldNote: He welcomes steady change and moves first, and he combines that with a clear view on fairness. He frames automation as taking the worst jobs, not the workers. His real fear is consolidation that strengthens the processors he already resents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public rules immediately, a share of the profit from robot labour going back to communities. I'd be loud on the forum, and I'd go to my representative's office in person. I'd say it isn't the machines I'm worried about, it's who owns them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big pig companies would have fully robotic barns within a year and the price per pig would collapse. My edge would be gone overnight, because everyone could buy what I spent ten years learning. With three months of savings and a finance plan, that's a real squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push ahead and automate everything I could in the first six months, because standing still would be worse. I'd cut every cost at home, starting with the trip to see our son overseas. I'd lobby with the farmers' union for a public fund to help small farms through it, and I'd try to keep the team on reduced hours rather than let anyone go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I'd still know what to do, but my chest would be tight for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been ahead of the curve. Does that still help you with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only partly. It helps that I know how these systems work and I can move quickly. But with two years, the big firms move quicker, and they have the money. Being early is no use if the rich arrive the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ingrid about the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we have to decide fast whether we're in or out, and I'd want us to be in, with machines bought together. She's more careful than me. She'd say let's not bet the farm, and she'd probably be right about half of it.

S2.say: He'd loudly call for public rules sharing robot profits with communities, visit his representative in person and stress that ownership of the machines is the real issue.
S2.think: Privately he expects big pig companies to automate within a year and prices to collapse, wiping out his ten-year edge, which with three months of savings and finance is a real squeeze.
S2.do: Automates everything he can in the first six months rather than stand still, and cuts household costs starting with a trip to see their son overseas. Lobbies with the union for a public fund for small farms and keeps his team on reduced hours.
S2.feel: Anxious with a tight chest for a year, but not panicked because he still knows what to do.
S2.quote: Being early is no use if the rich arrive the same day.
S2.fieldNote: Even this adaptive man is shaken by the speed, because it erases the head start he worked for. He responds by moving faster rather than freezing. He blames concentrated ownership rather than technology itself, which fits his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can still get this right if we start now, and I'd be pushing farmers to organise before the big firms do. I'd write on the forum that five years is enough to build co-operatives that own robots, if nobody wastes the first two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me. I'd be ahead of most farms, the finance paid down, and I'd be sixty-three with options. The pressure is real, but it's pressure I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate in stages, pen cleaning in the first year and feeding in the second, paying as I go instead of borrowing heavily. I'd help start a robot-sharing co-operative with six or seven pig farms in the area. And I'd keep writing to my representative about a profit-sharing law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the busy way. I'd feel stretched, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pacing. With two years I have to gamble on finance. With five I can buy one thing, learn it, pay it off, then buy the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the AI tools themselves during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day, like now, but more. I'd use them to plan the purchases, model the pig prices and write the co-operative's rules. I'm the one in our group who'd draft the paperwork with a program and then check every line.

S3.say: He'd urge farmers on the forum to organise before the big firms do, arguing that five years is enough to build co-operatives that own robots if nobody wastes the start.
S3.think: Privately five years suits him: he'd be ahead of most farms with finance paid down, sixty-three with options, facing pressure he's good at handling.
S3.do: Automates in stages, pen cleaning in year one and feeding in year two, paying as he goes. Helps start a robot-sharing co-operative with six or seven local pig farms and keeps writing to his representative about profit sharing.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a busy way, stretched rather than scared.
S3.quote: With five I can buy one thing, learn it, pay it off, then buy the next.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him pace investment and avoid heavy borrowing, which visibly lowers his stress. He sees himself as the organiser and paperwork person for other farmers. His politics and his appetite for technology work together here rather than pulling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse this time, and I'd push hard for public training money and shared ownership laws while there's time. I'd say it on the forum and at the union. Ten years is long enough to build something fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the best case for me. I'd automate gradually, hand over to Ingrid's son or to Sami by sixty-five, and step back. The farm would be worth more as a working robotic farm than as a tired old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invest steadily, a machine every couple of years, and get the farm running mostly on robots by about 2032. I'd plan to step back at sixty-five and sell my half to whoever takes over, probably over several years. And I'd keep training Sami so he can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to sixty-eight. Do you see yourself still farming then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want to be out by sixty-five, in the garden and on the phone telling Sami what he's doing wrong. Hanna has been waiting a long time for me to take a proper holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this slow version that bothers you more than the faster ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that people relax. Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's 2034 and nobody's done anything. I've seen that with every farm policy in my life.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse this time and push at the forum and the union for public training money and shared ownership laws while there's a decade to build something fair.
S4.think: Privately it's the best case for him: automate gradually, hand over by sixty-five and step back, with a robotic farm worth more than a tired one.
S4.do: Invests in a machine every couple of years to run mostly on robots by about 2032. Plans to step back at sixty-five and sell his half over several years, while training his young worker to run it.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels like a plan rather than a threat.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's 2034 and nobody's done anything.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he is fully at ease and treats AGI as a business transition. His one concern is political complacency, drawn from his long experience of farm policy. He's the rare farmer for whom more automation raises the value of what he'll hand on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because speed hands everything to whoever has the most money. What would help is a public fund that lends to small farms at low interest to buy machines, and a law that a share of robot profits goes back into the towns those jobs came from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. A robot can clean a pen, but someone has to decide what a good life for a pig is. I'd want that written into the rules before the machines decide it by default.

headlineQuote: A robot can clean a pen, but someone has to decide what a good life for a pig is.
portrait: Tomas Ziegler, 58, co-owns a pig and maize farm with his sister and leads a team of four, using AI tools every day while still walking the barns by nose. He's progressive, curious and comfortable with risk, and his anger is reserved for the meat processors and concentrated ownership rather than technology. He is calm through the plateau and steady change, anxious if AGI arrives in two years and erases his head start, and increasingly relaxed as the timeline stretches. With ten years he plans a gradual robotic transition and a handover by sixty-five.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because the speed hands everything to whoever has the most money and wipes out his head start.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund lending to small farms at low interest for machines, and a law returning a share of robot profits to the towns that lost the jobs.
